parole.testo: Ultimately derived from Vulgar Latin ācrus, from Classical Latin ācrem (with a change in declension). Likely borrowed from Gallo-Italic, mostly displacing the inherited and now rare acro. Cognate with Sicilian agru. Doublet of acre, a borrowing from Latin.

parole.significato: to arrive, to come, to reach
parole.testo: Inherited from Early Medieval Latin adrīpāre, perhaps influenced from Gallo-Italic or Old French in comparison to arripare. By surface analysis, a- + riva (“shore”) + -are.
Ultimately from Latin cunīculus. Judging by its /ʎʎ/, borrowed via a Western Romance language, perhaps some variety of Gallo-Italic. Doublet of cunicolo.

parole.significato: poor (with little or no possessions or money)
parole.testo: From Latin pauperem. Given that the expect native reflex would have been *popere, this form was likely among the early borrowings into Italian from Gallo-Italic.
From Vulgar Latin *pullētrus, from Latin pullus (“young animal”, whence Italian pollo), likely via a Gallo-Italic language, for expected polletro.

parole.significato: to receive, get, have, be given, take
parole.testo: From Latin recipere. Possibly borrowed from a Gallo-Italic language, where Latin /-p-/ > /v/ is a regular change, unlike in Italian. Compare the doublet recepire.
Inherited from Latin rīpa. In this specific form, on account of its /v/, perhaps influenced from Gallo-Italic or Old French.

Ultimately from Vulgar Latin *rōsāta, from Latin rōs, but borrowed, at least in the form rugiada, from some Gallo-Italic language. The form in question is first documented in the late thirteenth century, as are both of the more indigenous-looking variants above. More information As ⟨VgiV⟩ has since
